Tanvir, you keep saying you want to earn something on the side. Let your Jahnavi Bua tell you how I started, back in my second year of college.
I didn't begin with ideas. I sat on the hostel floor with a notebook and drew two columns. Left side: what can I actually do? Maths tutoring, neat handwriting, fast typing. Right side: where are my free hours? I went day by day. Classes till four, lab on Tuesday and Thursday, the long bus ride home every Saturday.
When I added it up, I had maybe eight free hours a week, not the twenty I'd imagined. So I crossed out the typing job that wanted afternoons, and kept tutoring two children in my own building on weekday evenings. It fit, and I never once had to cancel on them.
That's all I'm telling you, Tanvir. Count first, then choose.

qa.q: How many free hours a week did Jahnavi find when she added them up?
qa.a: Maybe eight free hours a week, not the twenty Jahnavi had imagined.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt when the count came to eight hours instead of twenty?
qa.a: Probably surprised and a little deflated, but also relieved to know the real number before promising anyone those hours.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the plan fit, and what else could Jahnavi have tried?
qa.a: Crossing out the afternoon typing job and keeping evening tutoring made it fit; Jahnavi could also have tried one trial week with the children before committing.

qa.q: What is it like for the two children's families that Jahnavi only promised hours she really had?
qa.a: They get a tutor who turns up reliably on weekday evenings and never cancels, which makes the arrangement easy to trust.

grounding: Shows a student listing skills and counting real free hours before choosing a side job that fits them.

The coaching centre wanted an answer by nine that night, and the hostel lights had gone out at seven. Payal sat on the stairwell with her phone torch and a torn page, Deepak beside her swatting mosquitoes.
'Just say yes,' he said. 'They pay per class.'
'Wait.' She wrote SKILLS and listed chemistry, spoken English, drawing diagrams. Under HOURS she went slowly. 'Classes end at three-thirty. Practicals Monday and Wednesday till six. Sunday I go home.' She counted aloud on her fingers. 'Tuesday, Thursday, Friday evenings. Six hours, tops.'
'They want four evenings.'
'Then I can't give them four evenings.'
At eight-forty she messaged the centre: three evenings, chemistry only. The reply came quickly: start with two, and we'll see. Payal wrote the new number under her list and felt her shoulders drop.

qa.q: What time did the coaching centre want an answer by?
What might Payal have been worried about as Deepak urged her to say yes?
qa.a: She was likely anxious about promising more evenings than she really had; her dropped shoulders at the end show relief.

qa.q: What else could Payal have done if the centre had refused anything less than four evenings?
qa.a: She could have looked for other tutoring on just Tuesday, Thursday and Friday evenings, so the work still matched the hours she counted.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak first sees it as overthinking a paid offer, then watches Payal turn a quick yes into a deal that fits her real week.

grounding: Shows a student listing her skills and counting the hours left after classes and practicals before accepting tutoring work.
